issues.name: Negligence – landlord's duty of care
issues.rule: Negligence requires duty, breach, actual and proximate cause, and damages. A landlord retains control of common areas and building systems and owes tenants and their invitees a duty of reasonable care to inspect for and repair or warn of dangerous conditions (modern rule: reasonable care to all foreseeable entrants).
keyFacts: Tenant rents space in a Cityville office building from Landlord
basement hallways and wiring are building-wide, not within Tenant's leased space
Tenant working late in the building
issues.analysis: Landlord controlled the basement, hallways and wiring serving all tenants, so he owed Tenant, a foreseeable plaintiff, a duty of reasonable care. Duty is clear.

issues.name: Breach – accumulated newspapers (actual knowledge)
issues.rule: Breach is failure to act as a reasonable person would; weigh burden of precaution against probability and gravity of harm (Learned Hand). A landlord with actual or constructive notice of a hazard in a common area must remedy it in reasonable time.
keyFacts: old newspapers left by a previous tenant three years ago
hallways nearly impassable
Landlord was aware of this, but hadn't gotten around to cleaning them up
fire marshal: newspapers a principal source of fuel
issues.analysis: Landlord knew of a large fire load for three years; removal was cheap and fire risk grave. Origin by a prior tenant is no excuse once Landlord had notice. Breach is very likely.

issues.name: Breach – faulty wiring (constructive notice / duty to inspect)
issues.rule: A landlord must make reasonable inspections of building systems; liability for a latent defect requires actual or constructive notice (defect existed long enough or reasonable inspection would reveal it).
keyFacts: Fire apparently originated in basement
Apparent cause: faulty wiring
no fact says Landlord knew of the wiring problem
issues.analysis: No fact shows Landlord knew of the wiring; Tenant must argue a reasonable inspection would have found it, and that the newspaper pile blocked inspection. Closer call than the newspapers, but breach still likely because of the newspapers.

issues.name: Negligence per se – hallway ordinance
issues.rule: Violation of a safety statute or ordinance establishes duty and breach if the plaintiff is in the protected class and the harm is of the type the statute was meant to prevent (Cal. Evid. Code 669 adds presumption of negligence; excuse is a rebuttal).
keyFacts: ordinance punishes permitting any article to remain in a hallway so as to impede entering or leaving
hallways nearly impassable
Tenant unconscious, carried out by firefighter
issues.analysis: Landlord violated the ordinance and Tenant is in the protected class (occupants needing egress), but the ordinance targets obstructed exit, not fire spread; Tenant was not blocked from leaving. Probably not the type of harm, but arguable (obstruction may have slowed rescue, and fuel load). Falls back on common-law breach.

issues.name: Res ipsa loquitur
issues.rule: Res ipsa permits inference of negligence when the harm ordinarily does not occur absent negligence, the instrumentality was in defendant's exclusive control, and plaintiff did not contribute.
keyFacts: building wiring and basement under Landlord's control
fire destroyed the building
issues.analysis: Fire from defective wiring in an area under Landlord's control supports an inference, an alternative way to prove breach if the wiring notice is doubtful.

issues.name: Actual cause
issues.rule: But-for: harm would not have occurred absent defendant's negligence (substantial factor where multiple causes).
keyFacts: Fire marshal: 'Apparent cause: faulty wiring'
newspapers 'probably resulted in rapid spread'
report is hedged ('apparently', 'probably')
issues.analysis: But for the newspapers and wiring neglect, the fire would not have spread so rapidly; the marshal's report is evidence, hedged language goes to weight. Satisfied.

issues.name: Proximate cause – fire, smoke inhalation and loss of contents
issues.rule: Defendant is liable for harms that are the foreseeable result of the risk his negligence created; pre-existing conditions are not superseding causes.
keyFacts: fire fed by newspapers
Tenant overcome by smoke
building and all its contents destroyed
wiring cause (not a superseding event)
issues.analysis: Fire spread, smoke injury and property destruction are exactly the foreseeable risks of faulty wiring plus a fuel pile. The prior tenant leaving the papers is not superseding.

issues.name: Proximate cause – broken leg (rescuer/ intervening negligence)
issues.rule: Rescue is foreseeable ('danger invites rescue'); negligence of rescuers in the course of rescue is a foreseeable, dependent intervening cause that does not cut off the original tortfeasor's liability (Landlord liable for aggravation). The firefighter's rule bars rescuers' suits, not the rescued party's.
keyFacts: firefighter found Tenant unconscious
while carrying Tenant out, dropped him, breaking Tenant's leg
issues.analysis: Firefighter's negligent drop is a foreseeable consequence of the fire, so not a superseding cause; Landlord is liable for the broken leg (Tenant may also sue the firefighter/city).

issues.name: Other theories – breach of lease covenants, nuisance, strict liability
issues.rule: Tenant might also plead breach of the lease/implied covenant of quiet enjoyment or habitability (weak for a commercial lease and fire), or nuisance; strict liability does not apply to a landlord's building fire.
keyFacts: Tenant rents space
lease relationship
issues.analysis: Negligence (and negligence per se) is the strongest theory; alternative theories add little and may be limited by the lease.

issues.name: Damages – personal injury (compensatory)
issues.rule: Compensatory damages place plaintiff in pre-tort position: medical expenses, lost earnings, and pain and suffering; plaintiff takes the injuries as they are (eggshell).
keyFacts: overcome by smoke, unconscious
broken leg
issues.analysis: Tenant recovers medical costs, lost income, and pain and suffering/emotional distress for smoke inhalation and the broken leg.

issues.name: Damages – property and economic loss
issues.rule: Property damage is measured by the fair market value of destroyed personal property (and consequential business loss if proved with certainty and foreseeable).
keyFacts: The building and all its contents were destroyed
Tenant working late (business use)
issues.analysis: Tenant can recover value of destroyed contents and provable business interruption losses; punitive damages are unlikely absent malice or conscious disregard (arguable given Landlord's knowledge of the hazard).

issues.name: Defenses – comparative negligence, assumption of risk
issues.rule: Plaintiff's own unreasonable conduct reduces recovery (pure comparative negligence in California); assumption of risk requires knowing, voluntary encounter of the risk.
keyFacts: Tenant was working late
no facts show Tenant knew of the wiring or newspapers
issues.analysis: No facts show Tenant fault or knowledge of the hazard; defenses fail.

notes: Check strength of constructive-notice analysis for the wiring and whether the negligence per se type-of-harm analysis is a close call. Res ipsa and lease-based theories were not argued by either answer.

issues.name: UCC Article 2 governs
issues.rule: The UCC Article 2 applies to transactions in goods (movable tangible things at identification).
keyFacts: 1939 Denny Wilson card
sale for $550
issues.analysis: A baseball card is a good, so Article 2 applies.

issues.name: Merchant status of Sara and Bill
issues.rule: A merchant deals in goods of the kind or by occupation holds himself out as having knowledge or skill peculiar to the goods (2-104); a casual collector is not.
keyFacts: Sara is a doctor who ... averaging 15 transactions a week
recognized expert in the 1939-50 era
Bill operates a store that regularly sells baseball cards
issues.analysis: Bill is clearly a merchant. Sara, though a doctor, regularly trades for profit and is a recognized expert, so she is probably a merchant too; this matters for the confirmation rule and 2-207.

issues.name: Formation of the oral contract – disputed offer and acceptance
issues.rule: Under UCC 2-204 a contract may be made in any manner showing agreement; an inquiry or invitation to negotiate is not an offer. Bill must prove the oral agreement by credible evidence.
keyFacts: Bill claims he phoned Sara and offered ... $550, and that Sara accepted
Sara: Bill only asked, 'Would you consider taking $550'
'Okay, send me something in writing'
issues.analysis: Bill's version is a contract; Sara's version could be an invitation and a non-committal 'Okay.' Credibility issue for the fact finder; Bill must prove an agreement and the writing does not itself prove it.

issues.name: Statute of frauds – UCC 2-201(1)
issues.rule: A contract for the sale of goods of $500 or more must be evidenced by a writing sufficient to show a contract, signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought, stating quantity.
keyFacts: $550 price (over $500)
Sara claims the phone agreement was unenforceable
Sara never signed anything
issues.analysis: The price exceeds $500, so the oral agreement is unenforceable against Sara unless an exception applies.

issues.name: Merchant confirmation exception – 2-201(2)
issues.rule: Between merchants, a written confirmation sufficient against the sender, received within a reasonable time, satisfies the statute against the recipient unless she objects in writing within 10 days of receipt. 'Signed' includes any symbol adopted to authenticate, such as a letterhead. It removes the SOF defense only; the sender must still prove the oral contract.
keyFacts: unsigned, typed letter confirming the contract, identifying the parties, the card and the price
letterhead identifying Beyer's Baseball Cards and Collectibles
Sara received and read the letter but did not respond
issues.analysis: Letterhead suffices as authentication, both are merchants, Sara read it and did not object, so the SOF defense fails. Bill still must prove the phone agreement actually occurred.

issues.name: Added term – certificate of authenticity (UCC 2-207)
issues.rule: Additional terms in a confirmation between merchants become part of the contract unless the offer limits acceptance, they materially alter it, or objection is made; silence does not assent to material new terms.
keyFacts: Seller shall provide a certificate of authenticity
Certificates cost $100 and significantly increase a card's value
the parties had not discussed this before
Sara did not respond
issues.analysis: The term is a material alteration (cost and value), so it is excluded despite Sara's silence. The contract is for an uncertified card.

issues.name: Breach – Sara sold the card to another buyer
issues.rule: Seller's failure to deliver or repudiation (2-610) is breach, giving buyer remedies under 2-711 and following.
keyFacts: Sara said she had sold the card to another party for $575
issues.analysis: If a contract exists, Sara breached by selling to someone else.

issues.name: Damages – market price minus contract price (2-713) and the $250 claim
issues.rule: Buyer's damages for non-delivery are market price at the time he learned of the breach less contract price, plus incidental and consequential damages (2-715), less expenses saved; the market must be for goods as contracted.
keyFacts: Bill sought $250 based on $800 FMV of a certified card
Sara resold for $575
contract price $550
issues.analysis: Because the certificate is not a term, market value is for an uncertified card (about $575 per the resale), so damages are about $25 plus incidental or provable consequential damages, not $250.

issues.name: Specific performance / buyer's other remedies
issues.rule: Specific performance or replevin is available for unique goods (2-716), but not against a good-faith purchaser who has taken delivery; buyer may also cover (2-712) and must mitigate.
keyFacts: a 1939 Denny Wilson card
Sara recognized expert, collectibles
Sara already sold the card
issues.analysis: A rare card may be unique, but Bill sues only for damages and the card was already sold, so equitable relief is unlikely.

issues.name: Incidental and consequential damages
issues.rule: Incidental costs (2-715(1)) and foreseeable consequential losses proven with certainty (2-715(2)).
keyFacts: no facts of expenses or lost resale
issues.analysis: No facts show these; Bill gets none unless he proves them.

notes: Both answers wrongly suggest the confirmation proves or binds the contract; 2-201(2) only removes the SOF defense. Reviewer should check the market-value/$25 computation.

issues.name: Defamation elements – defamatory statement
issues.rule: Defamation: a defamatory statement of or concerning plaintiff, published to a third party who understands it, with fault and damage. A statement is defamatory if it tends to harm reputation.
keyFacts: note: 'Ms. Smith is a cokehead'
photo of Shelly snorting cocaine that looks exactly like Cindy
Cindy campaigning for State Senate
issues.analysis: Calling a political candidate a cocaine user (with a photo) is defamatory.

issues.name: Of and concerning Cindy – mistaken identity photo
issues.rule: The statement must be understood by recipients as referring to the plaintiff; it can be by implication or extrinsic facts (photo identical to plaintiff).
keyFacts: photograph was very clear and looked exactly like Cindy
very few people know that Cindy has a twin
Newspaper reported it received the photograph of 'Cindy Smith'
issues.analysis: Readers would understand the caption/photo as Cindy; Debbie meant it to refer to Cindy, so the element is met against both defendants.

issues.name: Falsity and truth defense
issues.rule: Plaintiff public figure must prove falsity; truth is a defense, judged by the sting or gist as understood.
keyFacts: Ms. Smith is a cokehead
photo is genuinely of Shelly, who is addicted to cocaine
issues.analysis: Shelly (a Smith) used cocaine, but the statement as communicated (about Cindy) is false; Debbie's truth argument fails.

issues.name: Publication by Debbie and liability for Newspaper's republication
issues.rule: Publication is communication to a third party; the original defamer is liable for foreseeable republication.
keyFacts: Debbie sent the photo and anonymous note to Newspaper
the day before the election
Newspaper published the photograph
issues.analysis: Sending the note is itself publication; it was foreseeable that Newspaper would print it, so Debbie is liable also for the printed publication.

issues.name: Libel, damages and causation (loss of election)
issues.rule: Written defamation is libel with general damages presumed; in public-concern cases presumed and punitive damages need actual malice, otherwise actual damages must be proven; causation must connect the statement to the harm.
keyFacts: Cindy was very distressed
subsequently lost the election
published the day before the election
issues.analysis: Libel; against Debbie (actual malice) damages are presumed, and the timing supports causation of reputation and distress harm; proving the election loss was caused by the story is harder.

issues.name: Constitutional limits – public figure/public concern and actual malice (Debbie)
issues.rule: A public official or figure must prove actual malice (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard) by clear and convincing evidence (NYT v. Sullivan); candidates are public figures and speech about a candidate's fitness is a public concern.
keyFacts: Cindy is campaigning for election to State Senate
Debbie dislikes Cindy and does not want Cindy to win
Debbie sent the old photo of Shelly with 'Ms. Smith is a cokehead'
issues.analysis: Cindy is a public figure; Debbie knew the photo was of Shelly and that it would be taken as Cindy, so she acted with knowing falsity. Actual malice is met.

issues.name: Privileges asserted by Debbie
issues.rule: A qualified privilege (public interest, common interest) is lost by abuse, such as knowledge of falsity or malice.
keyFacts: Debbie anonymously sent to Newspaper to defeat Cindy
issues.analysis: Any privilege is abused because Debbie knew the charge was false and acted from spite.

issues.name: Newspaper – defamatory meaning, caption as question or opinion
issues.rule: Statements phrased as questions or opinions are actionable if they imply false assertions of fact.
keyFacts: 'Cokehead for State Senate?'
caption with clear photo
issues.analysis: The photo and caption imply that Cindy uses cocaine; not protected opinion.

issues.name: Newspaper – of and concerning, publication, republisher liability
issues.rule: One who republishes defamation is liable as a publisher, even if the source was another; honest mistake about identity is not a defense to the elements.
keyFacts: Newspaper published the photograph the same day
published to its readers
Newspaper unaware that Cindy had a twin
issues.analysis: Elements are met as to Newspaper because readers would think it is Cindy and republishers are treated as original publishers; the dispute is fault.

issues.name: Newspaper – fault: actual malice standard
issues.rule: As a public figure, Cindy must prove Newspaper knew the statement was false or had serious doubts (reckless disregard); negligence is insufficient; failure to investigate or reliance on an anonymous source alone is usually not reckless unless obvious reasons to doubt.
keyFacts: Newspaper unaware that Cindy had an identical twin sister
anonymous tip delivered the day before the election
photograph very clear and looked exactly like Cindy
Newspaper reported it received it anonymously
issues.analysis: Newspaper had no reason to doubt the clear photo and did not know of the twin; at most negligent verification, which is not actual malice. Rushing to print an anonymous tip is a closer call but probably not reckless. Cindy likely loses against Newspaper.

issues.name: Newspaper – damages and defenses
issues.rule: Without actual malice, no presumed or punitive damages; qualified privilege/newsworthiness for election reporting; California requires a retraction demand (Civ. Code 48a) to recover general damages from a newspaper.
keyFacts: Newspaper reported the photograph as 'Cindy Smith' received anonymously
election the next day
issues.analysis: Cindy cannot recover presumed damages and would struggle to show actual malice. Retraction statute may also limit recovery; privilege is secondary.

notes: Check the Debbie 'of and concerning' framing (intent to refer to Cindy) and the close call on Newspaper recklessness; the California retraction statute (Civ. Code 48a) was not raised by either answer.
